question: An 88-year-old man with autonomy for all activities of daily living and with a history of well controlled hypertension, antiplatelet atrial fibrillation and a prostate adenocarcinoma at 78 years of age, currently free of disease. He is brought to the emergency room for acute aphasia and right hemiparesis, 45 minutes before. What is the most correct attitude?

options.opa: Perform cranial CT and if there are no hemorrhagic lesions or other contraindications in the analytical, initiate intravenous thrombolysis immediately.
options.opb: Perform urgent cranial CT and if there is no bleeding initiate anticoagulation.
options.opc: Perform cranial CT and admission to the rehabilitation center, since their attitude will not differ regardless of whether the etiology is ischemic or hemorrhagic.
options.opd: Cranial CT is not necessary, although antiaggregation would be withdrawn.

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Acute aphasia and right hemiparesis -> suggestive of acute stroke -> high suspicion for ischemic or hemorrhagic etiology -> 80% CHAIN: Perform cranial CT -> to differentiate between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke -> crucial for treatment decision -> 90% CHAIN: Cranial CT shows no hemorrhagic lesions -> consider initiating intravenous thrombolysis -> if no contraindications present -> 85% CHAIN: Cranial CT reveals bleeding -> contraindication for thrombolysis -> consider alternative management -> 80% CHAIN: Cranial CT shows no bleeding -> consider initiating anticoagulation -> if indicated for underlying condition like atrial fibrillation -> 80%
analysis: Given the presentation of acute aphasia and right hemiparesis in an 88-year-old man, the most appropriate initial step is to perform a cranial CT to determine the etiology of the symptoms. This will help differentiate between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke, guiding further management decisions.
